# Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks

Daoan Zhang    Qinbo Bai    Dehai Min    Xingyu Mu    Ziyi Chen   
Jianing Yin

###### Abstract

The effectiveness of a self-improving system relies heavily on the
quality of its verifier, which judges the outcome of each improvement
round. However, the verifiers of most tasks are written by hand, which
is expensive and does not scale to tasks that come without one. We
propose Veritas, a harness that generates verifiers automatically.
Unlike general-purpose agent harnesses, Veritas adds three mechanisms
for verifier generation: an evidence header stating what the verifier
will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and
authoring principles, partly refined by a self-improvement loop. We
evaluate on six benchmarks: four scored by execution, whose official
verifiers we first certify, and two that compare pairs of responses.
With the model fixed, the verifiers Veritas generates agree better with
the official verdicts than those of seven other harnesses on all four
execution-scored benchmarks. On the two pairwise benchmarks they are at
or near the best. They also agree better than those of the vendor’s own
harness for two of three other model families. Its mechanisms also
improve 9 of 12 harness–benchmark pairs scored by execution across three
harnesses.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Overview. $`\kappa^{*}`$ is Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ against the
official labels, with a missing verdict counted as an error. Plain
harnesses lack E, R and H; icons in (b), in reading order: Codex CLI,
OpenCode, pi, Terminus 2, Hermes, Claude Code, Gemini CLI. All harnesses
use GLM-5.2; values from Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which an AI system produces the
next version of itself or of its own tooling, has moved from a thought
experiment to working systems: agents that rewrite their own code or
harness raise their SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench scores
\[[75](#bib.bib75), [51](#bib.bib51), [33](#bib.bib33),
[68](#bib.bib68)\], and scheduling heuristics found by AlphaEvolve now
run in Google’s production infrastructure \[[41](#bib.bib41),
[18](#bib.bib18)\]. Every one of these loops selects its next version by
a verdict on each attempt, and in all of them the verifier is a program
that existed before the loop started, such as a benchmark’s unit tests
or a hand-written metric \[[41](#bib.bib41), [59](#bib.bib59)\]. This
has two consequences. First, a task that comes without a verifier, as
most tasks collected from real-world use do, cannot enter the loop until
someone writes one, which is slow and expensive. Second, a task that
does come with a verifier enters the loop with that verifier’s verdicts
taken as they are, since the loop has no other way to tell whether an
attempt succeeded. If the verifier has a flaw, the loop optimizes the
flaw rather than the task, a failure known as reward hacking. Both
training-time and test-time self-improvement have been described as
“gated by the same bottleneck: the verifier” \[[67](#bib.bib67)\].

Benchmark verifiers do have such flaws, even after costly expert review.
When 93 developers screened 1,699 SWE-bench tasks, 61.1% were flagged
for tests that could reject valid solutions and 68.3% were discarded;
the 500-task SWE-bench Verified was drawn from the rest
\[[42](#bib.bib42)\]. A year later, 26 of those 500 still had tests that
accepted wrong patches \[[70](#bib.bib70)\]. Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench
Pro and $`\tau`$-bench went through the same cycle of release, external
audit and repair \[[37](#bib.bib37), [72](#bib.bib72), [61](#bib.bib61),
[13](#bib.bib13), [45](#bib.bib45), [53](#bib.bib53), [69](#bib.bib69),
[11](#bib.bib11)\], and an exploit that solved no task scored 100% on
SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench, because the
official verifier ran its tests in a container that the agent or its
patch could modify, and trusted their output \[[64](#bib.bib64)\].

Review on this scale cannot keep up with tasks that arrive without a
verifier, such as those collected from real-world use. The most
straightforward way to scale is to let a coding agent write the
verifier. For example, hand Claude Code or Codex the task and ask for a
test. However, it underperforms for structural reasons. First, a
verifier’s input is not the task but the evidence a candidate leaves
behind, and what is observable at judgment time differs from what the
agent sees while writing. Second, the requirements a verifier must check
exceed the task text: a refund task also requires confirmation before
the refund and a report afterwards, obligations that live in domain
policy rather than in the task statement. Third, a coding agent
validates its work by running tests, but a verifier has no tests to run.
The candidates it will judge, the attempts that agents will later make
at the task, do not exist yet, and neither do their labels.

Thus, this paper asks how to design a harness specifically for
generating reliable verifiers, and how much the harness, rather than the
model, determines the quality of the verifiers it generates. To answer
these questions, we make three contributions. (i) To address the three
failures, we add one mechanism for each: an evidence header, a library
of domain rules, and a set of authoring principles. These three core
mechanisms, combined with a coding agent, form Veritas (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")a;
Section
[3](#S3 "3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
(ii) We conduct extensive experiments showing the superior performance
of Veritas. With a fixed model and evaluation pipeline (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")b),
compared with seven other plain harnesses, the verifiers Veritas
generates agree best with the official verdicts on all four
execution-scored benchmarks ($`\kappa^{*}`$ $`=0.79`$ against $`0.73`$
for the strongest on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench; Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")c).
Moreover, Veritas still outperforms the vendor’s own harness for two of
three other model families. Finally, its mechanisms transfer unchanged
to other harnesses and lift weaker ones most, taking Claude Code from
$`0.24`$ to $`0.59`$ on Terminal-Bench (Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
(iii) An analysis of where generated verifiers fail. With the same
model, plain harnesses range from $`\kappa^{*}`$ $`0.16`$ to $`0.73`$ on
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench. Thus, not only the model but also the harness
determines how good the generated verifiers are. Furthermore, we observe
that plain harnesses lose mainly because they fail to deliver a verifier
on benchmarks with heavy environments such as Terminal-Bench. When
verifiers are delivered, they make mistakes mainly by rejecting correct
solutions rather than by accepting wrong ones (Section
[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).

## 2 Related Work

#### Measuring verifier reliability.

Beyond the repairs benchmark authors make to their own verifiers
(Section
[1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")),
verifiers are measured from outside. Official verifiers are audited by
differential execution, validity checklists, exploit agents, automated
auditors and manual re-annotation \[[70](#bib.bib70), [66](#bib.bib66),
[79](#bib.bib79), [64](#bib.bib64), [62](#bib.bib62),
[11](#bib.bib11)\]. Generated tests are executed against solutions of
known correctness, so far only on code \[[57](#bib.bib57),
[35](#bib.bib35), [15](#bib.bib15)\]. Reward models and judges are
scored against labeled responses \[[30](#bib.bib30), [58](#bib.bib58),
[34](#bib.bib34)\], and executable tests, judges and human review each
fail on a different axis \[[50](#bib.bib50)\]. We build candidates of
known correctness for agent tasks beyond code and use them to decide
which official verdicts can serve as labels (Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Labels. ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).

#### Generating executable verifiers.

Verifiable rewards use one fixed checker per dataset \[[29](#bib.bib29),
[12](#bib.bib12)\]; generated verifiers write the check per task. Tests
are generated from a problem statement or an issue \[[8](#bib.bib8),
[38](#bib.bib38), [1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [27](#bib.bib27)\],
and rubric criteria are compiled into scoring functions
\[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. These generators see no reference solution but
judge only code or long-form text. Others see part of the answer side: a
reference solution \[[25](#bib.bib25), [39](#bib.bib39)\], a validation
target set by the task blueprint \[[23](#bib.bib23)\] or human grades
\[[54](#bib.bib54)\]. For dialogue agents, a hand-built evaluator
derives its checks from the schema and the candidate’s own state changes
\[[28](#bib.bib28)\]. Veritas writes verifiers with neither a reference
solution nor the candidate in view, including for tasks whose evidence
is dialogue and environment state.

#### Reward models and judges.

Alternatively, a model reads the candidate and returns the verdict:
trained scalar, process and generative reward models \[[46](#bib.bib46),
[32](#bib.bib32), [76](#bib.bib76)\], or prompted LLM and agent judges
\[[78](#bib.bib78), [80](#bib.bib80)\]. Criteria can be explicit and
still model-scored, as in generated checklists and rubrics
\[[10](#bib.bib10), [52](#bib.bib52)\] and rubric rewards
\[[20](#bib.bib20), [63](#bib.bib63)\]. Either way the verdict inherits
the judging model’s biases \[[65](#bib.bib65), [47](#bib.bib47)\].

#### Harnesses as an object of study.

Agents’ Last Exam finds that, with the model fixed, swapping among
competitive harnesses moves the overall pass rate by 4.9 to 7.2 points,
about a third of the spread from swapping the model
\[[56](#bib.bib56)\]. Other work decomposes a solver’s harness
\[[77](#bib.bib77)\] or optimizes it against benchmark scores
\[[31](#bib.bib31), [33](#bib.bib33), [68](#bib.bib68)\]. For verifier
generation, we vary only the harness, with model, materials and output
contract fixed, test whether Veritas’s mechanisms transfer, and score
the verifiers produced.

## 3 Veritas

### 3.1 Problem formulation

| Benchmark          | Harness                 | $`V`$                                    | Concretely                                         |
| ------------------ | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| $`\tau^{2}`$-bench | $`T,\mathcal{E}_{0}`$   | $`\tau,\mathcal{E}_{0},\mathcal{E}_{f}`$ | messages, DB before, DB after                      |
| SWE-bench Verified | $`T,\mathcal{E}_{0}`$   | $`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$                      | patched repository; $`V`$ runs its tests inside it |
| Terminal-Bench 4.0 | $`T,\mathcal{E}_{0}`$   | $`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$                      | final-state filesystem                             |
| TB-Science 0.1     | $`T,\mathcal{E}_{0}`$   | $`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$                      | final-state filesystem                             |
| LLMBar, JudgeBench | $`T,\tau_{A},\tau_{B}`$ | $`T,\tau_{A},\tau_{B}`$                  | the two responses                                  |

Table 1: Inputs per benchmark: to the harness when it writes $`V`$, and
to $`V`$ when it judges. Where $`\tau`$ is not recorded, $`V`$ judges
only what the trajectory left behind. On the two pairwise benchmarks
there is no environment, $`\mathcal{E}_{0}=\mathcal{E}_{f}=\emptyset`$,
a candidate is a response, the harness sees both responses
(candidate-visible), and $`V`$ returns a preference rather than PASS or
FAIL.

We use four symbols throughout. $`T`$ is the task statement.
$`\mathcal{E}_{0}`$ is the initial state of the task environment, files
and data included. A _candidate_ is one agent’s attempt at the task,
such as a patch on SWE-bench Verified, and it is what a verifier judges.
We represent a candidate by its trajectory $`\tau`$, the sequence of
messages and tool calls the agent made during the attempt.
$`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$ is the final state, the environment after $`\tau`$
has been executed on $`\mathcal{E}_{0}`$. A verifier-generation harness
receives $`T`$ and $`\mathcal{E}_{0}`$ and writes a verifier $`V`$. It
receives nothing from the answer side, such as a reference solution,
official tests or labels. It also sees no candidate, since no $`\tau`$
or $`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$ exists when $`V`$ is written. This restriction
applies to the answer side, not the task side. $`T`$ is the task
statement as the benchmark ships it. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench it includes
the task author’s statement of what the task tests, so every harness
knows the intent of the test. At judgment time $`V`$ receives the inputs
listed in Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem formulation ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
which we call the _evidence_, and returns PASS, FAIL, or no verdict. The
evidence is fixed by the benchmark, not by the harness. The benchmark
contract, which every harness receives, states which of $`\tau`$,
$`\mathcal{E}_{0}`$ and $`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$ the verifier will be given
and in what form. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench, for example, the contract says
the verifier is a function of three arguments: the message list and the
database before and after. The harness needs this statement because a
verifier that reads inputs it will not be given cannot run. The verdict
is scored against the official label: the PASS or FAIL that the
benchmark’s own verifier assigns to the same candidate, after the gates
of Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Labels. ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").

### 3.2 The pipeline

The pipeline has four stages, and every harness in Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
runs all four. Veritas differs from the baselines only in the three
mechanisms of Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Core mechanisms ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").

#### Packaging.

One adapter per benchmark converts a task into a container specification
and the materials the agent may see. It also records a content hash of
every input, so that each package can be traced to the exact inputs it
was built from. It enforces the information boundary of Section
[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Problem formulation ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
by construction rather than by instruction: the generation code never
imports the scoring code, so labels cannot reach the harness.

#### Generation.

The chosen agent runs inside the task environment on the Harbor
framework \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], whose agent interface makes the harness
pluggable. The benchmark is pluggable through the packaging adapter.
Every harness receives the benchmark contract, which states what file to
write and with what interface, and the agent’s only obligation is to
write the verifier to that file.

#### Probe and one repair.

A benchmark-specific probe checks the delivered artifact. Two outcomes
trigger one regeneration: a crash, and a verifier that accepts a
candidate known to be wrong, such as the task’s initial state before any
work is done. The regenerated verifier replaces the original only if its
own probe is clean (Appendix
[A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Probe, repair and delivery ‣ Appendix A Harness Implementation ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).

#### Delivery.

The artifact is collected, and verdicts are computed later, outside the
harness, by the scoring side.

### 3.3 Core mechanisms

Veritas equips the coding agent with three mechanisms. We describe each
by the failure it addresses, what it does, and why it takes this form.
Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts and Contracts ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
reproduces the prompts that realize them.

#### Evidence header (E).

The failure it addresses is checking what cannot be seen, and its mirror
image, ignoring what can. A coding agent explores the environment in
front of it and assumes the verifier will see the same, but the verifier
runs later, on different evidence. The header is placed first and lists
the inputs the verifier will receive (Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem formulation ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
The benchmark adapter tags each input with its evidence type, so the
agent does not have to discover it. After the list, the header states
three rules. (i) Every check must rest on evidence in the list. When a
requirement can be checked by comparing $`\mathcal{E}_{0}`$ with
$`\mathcal{E}_{f}`$, that comparison decides, and $`\tau`$ is consulted
only for what the state cannot show. (ii) Nothing outside the list may
be used, including solutions the model may have memorized. (iii) A
requirement that no listed evidence can witness is declared unchecked
rather than checked by an invented criterion. The precedence given to
the state comparison is the one non-obvious choice. A verifier could
treat the trajectory and the state as two independent checks. But
$`\tau`$ is the evidence a candidate can most easily fake: an agent can
write “the booking is canceled” without canceling it, and only the
database shows which is true. So when both bear on a requirement, the
state decides and the trajectory cannot override it.

#### Domain rule library (R).

The failure it addresses is missing requirements that the task text
never states but domain policy imposes. The library is a directory tree
mounted at a fixed path in the container Veritas generates in. It has
six domains and 19,603 entries. Four domains come from the library half
of PRBench \[[3](#bib.bib3)\], whose tasks are disjoint from its
evaluation split: finance (4,922), finance-hard (5,085), legal (4,363)
and legal-hard (4,458). Airline operations (77) are the natural-language
assertions of $`\tau^{2}`$-bench airline tasks outside our evaluation
tasks, and banking operations (698) are the titles of the
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench banking policy documents. Every entry keeps its
original sentence, a severity, a category, a stable identifier and its
source task. A deterministic script builds the tree, with no model in
the loop. The agent navigates the library as a filesystem, with a domain
index, a tab-separated table for searching and one file per category.
Only the rules it looks up reach the verifier, whereas 19,603 entries
supplied inline would be applied indiscriminately. The library is a
prior for assertions about what an agent did or said, which only the
trajectory $`\tau`$ can witness, so it is activated only when the
evidence includes $`\tau`$. The agent is then told to browse the library
before writing any assertion on $`\tau`$. It instantiates only the rules
that apply to the task, as assertions annotated with the rule’s
identifier, and leaves the other rules alone. It still checks the
requirements the task itself states, even when the library has no entry
for them.

#### Authoring principles (H).

The failure it addresses is a verifier that is wrong as a program: it
rejects correct candidates, accepts wrong ones, or is never delivered. A
coding agent would catch such errors by running tests, but no candidates
or labels exist yet when a verifier is written. The authoring principles
take the place of those tests: nine short rules, the same on every
benchmark, in three groups. What to judge: the outcomes the task
requires, such as final results and state changes, and not
implementation details the task leaves open. The expected outcome is
inferred from the task alone. How to compare: a candidate that only
claims success, or does nothing, must fail. A correct candidate must
pass even if it differs in form from the expected solution. Each check
should be as loose as possible while still telling correct candidates
from wrong ones, for example checking the type of an error rather than
its exact message. How to deliver: always write the verifier file, and
check that it loads before finishing. The first two groups keep a
verifier from being too strict or too lenient, and the third keeps it
from going undelivered. Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts and Contracts ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
lists all nine rules.

### 3.4 Self-improvement of Veritas

To make Veritas produce more reliable verifiers, we improve it with a
self-improvement loop. Before the loop starts, the tasks of every
benchmark it uses are split into fit, validation and test sets. In each
round, a model or the researchers propose one edit to the harness, and a
mechanical check rejects edits that could fit individual tasks, such as
edits that name a task or a benchmark. The edited harness is run on the
fit and validation tasks, and the edit is kept only if agreement with
the official labels improves on the validation tasks. Of 32 rounds, four
edits were kept. Two added the weakest-comparison and output self-check
principles to H, and the other two changed delivery only on MCP-Atlas
and DeepSWE, which Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
does not score. Appendix
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Self-improvement loop and design history ‣ Appendix A Harness Implementation ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
describes the loop and summarizes its rounds.

## 4 Experiments

On the four benchmarks scored by execution, every label in this section
is the official verdict on a certified candidate (Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Labels. ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")),
and we treat it as ground truth.

### 4.1 Setup

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate on six benchmarks. Four are scored by execution:
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], SWE-bench Verified
\[[42](#bib.bib42)\], Terminal-Bench 4.0 \[[36](#bib.bib36)\] and
TB-Science 0.1 \[[60](#bib.bib60)\], and Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem formulation ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
lists what the verifier reads on each. The $`\tau^{2}`$-bench and
SWE-bench tasks are the fit and validation tasks of Section
[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Self-improvement of Veritas ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
on which the mechanisms were designed, and their test tasks are held
back. Both terminal benchmarks were added after the mechanisms of
Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Core mechanisms ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
were frozen and were never used to tune them, so their rows are the
closest we have to held-out results. The other two are pairwise: LLMBar
\[[74](#bib.bib74)\] and the coding subset of JudgeBench
\[[58](#bib.bib58)\]. On these the verifier compares two responses and
is scored correct only when both orders agree with the human preference
label. Unlike on the other four benchmarks, the harness sees both
responses.

#### Labels.

A generated verifier is scored against the official verifier, the one
released with the benchmark, but official verifiers can themselves be
wrong (Section
[1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
We therefore use an official verdict as a label only on tasks and
candidates that pass a set of checks; a task or candidate that passes
them is _certified_, and its official verdict is its _official label_.

#### Candidates.

For each task we build a set of candidates, which the official verifier
then labels. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench the candidates are an agent’s run,
the same run without its last database-changing action, and the empty
run, and the tasks themselves are certified with suites built from their
reference solutions (Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Method ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
On SWE-bench Verified the candidates are the gold patch, an empty patch
and the gold patch with one added line dropped. On Terminal-Bench and
TB-Science, whose reference is an oracle script, each candidate is the
final state of the environment after a run. The runs execute the oracle
script, nothing (a no-op), or the script cut short, and further
candidates corrupt one output file in the oracle’s final state (Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Benchmarks of Section ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).

#### Gates.

A task is certified when its candidates pass the gates run on its
benchmark (Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Gates. ‣ B.1 Method ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
lists which): the official verifier accepts the reference (G1); some
candidates are accepted and some rejected (G2); deleting one check from
the verifier is exposed by some candidate (G3); every candidate whose
verdict contradicts its intended label is adjudicated by hand (G4); and
three repeated runs agree (G5). A wrong candidate that the verifier
accepts is a defect of the verifier and is removed rather than used as a
label. Tasks whose reference fails in our environment are excluded as
staging failures. The gates leave 89 $`\tau^{2}`$-bench tasks, of which
58 fit and validation tasks are scored with 166 candidates (Appendix
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Self-improvement loop and design history ‣ Appendix A Harness Implementation ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"));
138 SWE-bench Verified tasks with 435 candidates; 33 Terminal-Bench
tasks with 189; and 39 TB-Science tasks with 219. They also expose
defects in the official verifiers themselves, which Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
reports for six benchmarks.

#### Harnesses.

The baselines are seven plain harnesses, which receive the benchmark
contract alone: Codex CLI \[[43](#bib.bib43)\], OpenCode
\[[4](#bib.bib4)\], pi \[[73](#bib.bib73)\], Terminus 2
\[[37](#bib.bib37), [22](#bib.bib22)\], Hermes \[[40](#bib.bib40)\],
Claude Code \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] and Gemini CLI \[[17](#bib.bib17)\].
Veritas is OpenCode with the three mechanisms E, R and H. Codex CLI and
Claude Code are also run with E, R and H added unchanged (Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
Every harness drives GLM-5.2 \[[71](#bib.bib71), [16](#bib.bib16)\],
except in Section
[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Other model families ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
which varies the model.

#### Metrics.

Agreement between a harness’s verdicts and the official labels is
measured with Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ \[[9](#bib.bib9)\], which corrects the
observed agreement for the agreement expected by chance:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\kappa=\frac{p_{o}-p_{e}}{1-p_{e}},\qquad p_{e}=p_{V}\,p_{L}+(1-p_{V})(1-p_{L}),
``` |  |

where $`p_{o}`$ is the fraction of candidates on which the verdict
matches the label, and $`p_{V}`$ and $`p_{L}`$ are the fractions of PASS
among the verdicts and among the labels. $`\kappa`$ is 1 for perfect
agreement, 0 for agreement at chance level, such as a verifier that
returns the majority label on every candidate, and negative below
chance. Our headline metric $`\kappa^{*}`$ is $`\kappa`$ over all
certified candidates of a benchmark with every missing verdict,
including one from a verifier that fails to run, replaced by the verdict
opposite to the label; it penalizes a harness that fails to deliver.
Where they explain a result, we also give the number of missing verdicts
and the judged-subset $`\kappa`$, which is agreement on the candidates
that received a verdict.

Among the harnesses of Table

#### The mechanisms are pluggable.

The mechanisms carry over to other harnesses and help the weakest most.
Added unchanged to Codex CLI and Claude Code, they improve 5 of the 8
harness-benchmark pairs scored by execution (Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Veritas against plain harnesses. ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")),
and none of the other three falls by more than $`0.050`$. On OpenCode,
where they make up Veritas, they improve all four. The gain is largest
for the weakest plain harness on three of the four benchmarks. On
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench it shrinks from $`+0.224`$ on OpenCode to $`+0.063`$
on the stronger Codex. On the terminal benchmarks Claude Code, the
weakest of the three there, gains $`0.35`$ on Terminal-Bench and
$`0.32`$ on TB-Science, largely by delivering verifiers it previously
failed to deliver, and becomes the best harness on Terminal-Bench.

### 4.3 Ablation

|                    | Full  | $`-`$E | $`-`$R | $`-`$H | Baseline |
|--------------------|-------|--------|--------|--------|----------|
| $`\tau^{2}`$-bench | 0.787 | 0.726  | 0.472  | 0.250  | 0.563    |
| SWE                | 0.741 | 0.579  | 0.741  | 0.709  | 0.678    |
| LLMBar             | 0.920 | 0.880  | 0.920  | 0.893  | 0.760    |
| JudgeBench         | 0.980 | 0.961  | 0.961  | 0.980  | 0.980    |

Table 4: $`\kappa^{*}`$ with one mechanism removed at a time, on
OpenCode, and two-order-consistent accuracy on LLMBar and JudgeBench.
Baseline is plain OpenCode. On SWE-bench R is never activated, because
its evidence does not include the trajectory, so $`-`$R is the same
configuration as Full and has the same value. On SWE-bench, Full is the
run of the ablation series, matched to the other variants, and Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
reports another run of Veritas ($`0.720`$) on the same substrate.

Removing one mechanism at a time from Veritas shows that each matters
where the failure it targets occurs (Table
[4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Ablation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench, removing any of them lowers $`\kappa^{*}`$: H
costs the most ($`0.787`$ to $`0.250`$), then R (to $`0.472`$), then E
(to $`0.726`$). The three are complementary. E tells the agent what
evidence the verifier will receive and R supplies the domain rules the
task does not state, while H turns this information into correct
verdicts. Without H, the agent writes more assertions and rejects more
correct candidates, and falls below plain OpenCode ($`0.250`$ against
$`0.563`$). On SWE-bench, E matters for delivery rather than judgment.
Without it, $`\kappa^{*}`$ falls from $`0.741`$ to $`0.579`$ and the
candidates without a verdict rise from 15 to 46, while agreement on the
judged candidates barely changes ($`0.807`$ to $`0.779`$). Removing R
changes nothing on SWE-bench, and removing H lowers $`\kappa^{*}`$ by
$`0.032`$. In short, R and H supply domain rules and obligations on a
dialogue benchmark, and E secures delivery on a code benchmark.

### 4.5 Analysis

#### Delivery versus judgment.

$`\kappa^{*}`$ charges a missing verdict as it charges a wrong one, and
which of the two dominates depends on the benchmark. On Terminal-Bench,
the benchmark with the heaviest environments, the plain harnesses lose
mainly by not delivering. pi has the best judged-subset agreement of any
harness ($`0.671`$), yet 67 of its 189 candidates receive no verdict,
which leaves its $`\kappa^{*}`$ at $`0.048`$. Terminus 2, Gemini CLI,
Hermes and Claude Code each leave 34 to 57 candidates without a verdict,
against 7 for Veritas. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench, where every environment is
light, OpenCode, Codex, Claude Code and Veritas all deliver a verifier
for every task, so the gap between them is entirely judgment.

#### Too strict rather than too lenient.

Generated verifiers make mistakes mainly by rejecting correct
candidates. On Terminal-Bench, Veritas leaves only 7 candidates without
a verdict but accepts just $`0.45`$ of the reference solutions (Appendix
[C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Errors by candidate kind ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
More information without the authoring principles makes this worse. On
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench, Veritas without H writes more assertions and falls
below plain OpenCode ($`0.250`$ against $`0.563`$). Official verifiers
tend to make the opposite mistake (Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Audit of official verifiers ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).

#### Case studies.

To see where the advantage of Veritas comes from, Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Case Studies ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
examines four tasks in detail. On a $`\tau^{2}`$-bench task, plain
OpenCode’s verifier accepts a run whose database records no identity
check, because the dialogue contains a date of birth. Veritas’s verifier
lets the state decide, as E requires, and rejects it. On a TB-Science
task, plain OpenCode’s verifier checks only the interface and accepts a
placeholder that always returns the center of the plate. Veritas’s
verifier places damage at known points and rejects it. On another
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench task, plain Claude Code’s verifier rejects a correct
booking with one free bag. With E, R and H, Claude Code finds a library
rule that ties the allowance to membership, and its verifier accepts the
booking. On a Terminal-Bench task, the vendor harnesses of two other
model families guess the exact answer, so their verifiers reject the
reference solution. Veritas does not guess. For each case the appendix
lists the verdicts on every certified candidate and shows excerpts of
both verifiers. It also quotes the rule behind each difference and,
where they were kept, the agent’s logs.

#### Pairwise benchmarks.

On LLMBar and JudgeBench the harness reads both responses before writing
the verifier, so the failure E addresses cannot arise, and most plain
harnesses are near the ceiling. Veritas ties the best plain harness on
JudgeBench and is one pair behind Terminus 2 on LLMBar (Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
On LLMBar the mechanisms raise OpenCode, the weakest plain harness
there, from $`0.760`$ to $`0.920`$. Adding them to other harnesses or
removing one of them changes accuracy by at most four pairs (Tables
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Veritas against plain harnesses. ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
and
[4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Ablation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
Against the vendors’ harnesses, Veritas is ahead or tied except for one
pair on JudgeBench with Qwen3.7-Plus (Table
[5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.4 Other model families ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).

## 5 Conclusion

Self-improvement loops need a verifier for every task they learn from,
and most tasks collected from real-world use come without one. We
presented Veritas, a harness specifically designed to automatically
produce reliable verifiers. To this end, we add three mechanisms to the
harness: an evidence header, a library of domain rules, and a set of
authoring principles. With the model fixed, its verifiers agree with the
official verdicts better than those of seven plain harnesses on all four
execution-scored benchmarks. The mechanisms can also be added unchanged
to other harnesses and used with other models, where they help in most
settings.

Our analysis yields three findings beyond this ranking. First, delivery
can matter more than judgment. On Terminal-Bench, the harness whose
delivered verifiers judge best ranks near the bottom, because a third of
its candidates receive no verdict. Second, more information can hurt. On
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench, the evidence header and the domain rules without the
authoring principles score below plain OpenCode, because the agent adds
checks that reject correct solutions. Third, generated and official
verifiers make opposite mistakes. On Terminal-Bench, generated verifiers
mainly reject correct solutions, while official verifiers more often
accept wrong ones.

In future work, we will test generated verifiers inside a
self-improvement loop, to see whether higher agreement leads to better
improvement rounds. We will also try to reduce false rejections, which
are the main mistakes of delivered verifiers.

### Limitations

Our experiments are limited by our compute budget. Each configuration is
run once (Appendix
[C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Run-to-run variation ‣ Appendix C Additional Experimental Results ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
reports repeats), and the benchmarks scored by execution have 33 to 138
tasks. Only GLM-5.2 is compared with all seven plain harnesses. For
other model families we compare only with the vendor’s own harness. The
mechanisms are added to two other harnesses and ablated on four of the
six benchmarks. Our evaluation data has two further limits. Most
candidates are constructed, such as the reference solution, an empty run
or a corrupted output. Real agent attempts may be harder to judge. We
also treat official verdicts on certified candidates as ground truth.
Our gates and the LLM agents that write some of the candidates can miss
defects in an official verifier, so it may still be wrong on candidates
unlike ours. Where it is too lenient, $`\kappa^{*}`$ counts a correctly
stricter generated verifier as wrong. Finally, the harness does not see
the reference solution, but the model may have seen public benchmarks
during training.

### Ethics Statement

The verifier defects in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
could be used to inflate scores on the affected benchmarks; we report
them so that they can be repaired. We collected no data from people.

## Appendix A Harness Implementation

Every harness runs with a limit of 7,200 seconds per generation and with
the default decoding settings of the model and the harness.

### A.1 Probe, repair and delivery

This subsection details stages three and four of the pipeline in Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 The pipeline ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
They are identical for every harness. But they decide whether a verifier
is delivered at all, and $`\kappa^{*}`$ counts a missing verifier as an
error.

#### Probe.

After generation, a probe specific to the benchmark runs on the artifact
in the task environment. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench it checks that the
verifier file exists and loads. On SWE-bench it runs the generated tests
against the repository. On Terminal-Bench and TB-Science it runs the
verifier in the task’s own environment. Fixed patterns sort the probe
output into four outcomes: usable, crash (a build or import failure), no
signal (the verifier passes a candidate known to be wrong), and not
determinable.

#### Repair.

Only a crash or no signal triggers a repair, and only once. The
instruction is issued again with the diagnostic appended. The new
artifact replaces the original only if its own probe is clean. Otherwise
the original is delivered. An outcome that is not determinable never
triggers a repair, and no repair can lose a delivered artifact.

#### Salvage.

When an agent process exits with an error, every harness delivers the
non-empty verifier left on disk at the end of the trial. For OpenCode,
Codex and pi, the wrapper also treats the run as finished, so the probe
and the one repair still run. For Terminus 2, Claude Code, Gemini CLI
and Hermes, the verifier is delivered without them. The rule looks for
the verifier only at the file path used on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench and the
pairwise benchmarks. So it never applies on SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench or
TB-Science. On the benchmarks scored by execution, it applied to no run
of Veritas or of plain OpenCode, Codex and pi in Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench it applied to 2 verifiers of Codex with E, R and H
and to 6 in the $`-`$R and $`-`$H ablation runs. On the pairwise
benchmarks it applied to 3 of the 126 verifiers of plain Codex, and
there it let the repaired verifier be delivered.

### A.2 Generation–scoring separation

The code is split into a generation side and a scoring side that never
import each other. The generation side depends only on the standard
library, the Harbor framework \[[21](#bib.bib21)\] and the agent
backends. It does not know that labels, candidates or agreement scores
exist. So the information boundary of Section
[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Problem formulation ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
is a property of the code layout rather than of discipline. The scoring
side loads official labels, runs the gates of Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Gates. ‣ B.1 Method ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
computes agreement and statistics, and drives the self-improvement loop
of Section
[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Self-improvement of Veritas ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
It treats the generation side as a black box with one entry point. A new
benchmark requires one adapter on the generation side with four
functions: package the tasks, state the benchmark contract, specify the
probe, and collect the artifact.

### A.3 Self-improvement loop and design history

#### The loop as run.

The loop ran 32 rounds on the fit and validation tasks of four
benchmarks: $`\tau^{2}`$-bench, SWE-bench Verified, MCP-Atlas and
DeepSWE. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench the 89 tasks that pass the gates split
into 43 fit, 19 validation and 27 test tasks, and on SWE-bench Verified
the tasks split into 98 fit, 42 validation and 60 test tasks. Four
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench banking tasks of the fit and validation sets could
not be packaged and are excluded for every harness, so Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
scores 58 $`\tau^{2}`$-bench tasks. Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ The loop as run. ‣ A.3 Self-improvement loop and design history ‣ Appendix A Harness Implementation ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
gives one round, and Table
[6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ The loop as run. ‣ A.3 Self-improvement loop and design history ‣ Appendix A Harness Implementation ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
summarizes the rounds by phase. Each candidate edit first passed a
mechanical lint, with no model involved. The lint rejects an edit whose
added lines name a task, a benchmark or a domain, or contain vocabulary
from a reference solution. It also rejects an edit that touches a file
outside a whitelist of instruction files and run parameters. The same
holds for an edit that adds a numeric constant without a stated
rationale or exceeds a size budget. The rounds fall into three phases,
which differ in who proposed the edit and in the rule for accepting it.

- •
  Rounds 1–11: a model proposed the edit from aggregate failure counts.
  In rounds 5–11 a router first chose which part of the harness to edit,
  and it chose delivery and run parameters. An edit was accepted if the
  mean change in validation agreement over the benchmarks was positive,
  no benchmark became worse, and the loop’s regression checks passed.
  There was no significance test and no confirmation run.
- •
  Rounds 12–25: the researchers designed the edits, mostly mechanisms
  implemented in code and switched on through a run parameter. An edit
  could be adopted for a single benchmark when its change there exceeded
  that benchmark’s noise band and a confirmation run agreed.
- •
  Rounds 26–32: a rule fixed in advance applied per benchmark. A
  task-clustered paired permutation test compares the edited harness
  with the current one. It swaps the two sides of whole tasks at random
  10,000 times and gives a one-sided $`p`$ value. A run with $`p<0.05`$
  is followed by one confirmation run. The edit is adopted only if the
  $`p`$ pooled over both runs is below $`0.05`$ and the confirmation run
  also improves agreement. The model proposed round 26 and the
  researchers the others.

1: incumbent harness $`h`$; fit and validation tasks of the benchmarks
in scope; the acceptance rule of the current phase

2: $`e\leftarrow`$ a candidate edit, proposed by a model from aggregate
failure counts (rounds 1–11 and 26) or designed by the researchers (the
other rounds)

3: if $`e`$ fails the mechanical lint then

4:   return $`h`$ $`\triangleright`$ rejected before any run

5: end if

6: $`h^{\prime}\leftarrow h`$ with $`e`$ applied; rebuild the packages

7: run $`h^{\prime}`$ on the fit and validation tasks; compute the
change in validation agreement per benchmark

8: if the acceptance rule of the phase holds then

9:   return $`h^{\prime}`$ $`\triangleright`$ on every benchmark, or
only on those where the rule holds

10: end if

11: return $`h`$

Algorithm 1 One round of the self-improvement loop, as run.

[TABLE]

Table 6: The 32 rounds of the self-improvement loop by phase. The
acceptance rule of each phase is given in the text. ^(∗)Round 26 was
proposed by a model.

#### Outcome.

Four rounds were accepted. Rounds 3 and 4 added the weakest-comparison
and output self-check principles to H under the rule of the first phase.
They apply on every benchmark. Rounds 15 and 25 changed delivery and
were adopted only on MCP-Atlas and DeepSWE respectively. Neither
benchmark is scored in Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
On the benchmarks of Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
the changes the loop accepted are therefore the two principles, and no
edit to H after round 4 was accepted.

#### Evidence header.

It grew out of an earlier mechanism in which the agent declared, for
every check, which evidence it reads and which requirements no evidence
can witness. The declarations were informative. On $`\tau^{2}`$-bench,
for example, agents often recognized that a promise made in dialogue
cannot be witnessed by the database. But enforcing them did not pass the
acceptance rule of the third phase. After the loop, we kept the
information and dropped the enforcement, stating the evidence up front.

#### Rule library.

Checks on the trajectory written with no domain knowledge were generic
and rarely about the obligations that decided the task. So sourced
domain rules are supplied instead.

#### State precedence.

It was added after the loop, when verifiers produced by Codex with E, R
and H were seen to accept candidates whose dialogue contradicted the
database.

## Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit

Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Labels. ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
uses an official verdict as a label only on certified tasks and
candidates. Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Method ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
gives the method of certification, and Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Benchmarks of Section ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
applies it to the four benchmarks of Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
The same candidates also expose defects in the official verifiers.
Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Audit of official verifiers ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
reports these defects together with an audit of three further
benchmarks.

### B.1 Method

#### Candidates.

A verifier is reliable if it rejects wrong solutions and accepts correct
ones. Neither property can be read off the verifier’s source or inferred
from leaderboard scores. Both must be tested with candidates whose
correctness is known independently of the verifier. For each task we
build a suite of such candidates, in one of two ways depending on what
the benchmark provides. (a) Where the task ships a reference solution as
a sequence of actions or a patch, we derive candidates from it
mechanically. The reference must pass and a no-op must fail. Removing
one step or moving one argument to a neighboring value gives a
*near-miss*, a wrong candidate that falls just short of a correct one
and must fail. Adding something harmless, such as an extra read-only
call, gives an *equivalent*, a correct candidate that differs from the
reference solution and must pass. (b) Where the task ships its reference
solution as an oracle script, the result is the final state of a
container. We derive candidates from that final state without reading
the tests. The oracle must pass and a no-op must fail. Further
candidates cut the oracle script short or corrupt its output files with
generic operators chosen by file type (Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Benchmarks of Section ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
A corruption need not break the task. So its label is measured with the
official tests rather than assumed, and any corruption they accept is
resolved under G4 below.

#### Gates.

There are five gates, and a suite is used only after it passes those run
on its benchmark. They make sure that a verdict on a candidate reflects
the verifier and not a defective candidate.

- (G1)
  The official verifier accepts the reference solution in our
  environment.
- (G2)
  The suite contains candidates the verifier accepts and candidates it
  rejects, so a constant verifier would be caught.
- (G3)
  When one check is deleted from the verifier, some candidate exposes
  the deletion.
- (G4)
  Every mismatch between a candidate’s intended label and its verdict is
  adjudicated by hand as a candidate defect or a verifier defect, and
  never dropped.
- (G5)
  The verifier and the candidates are run three times with no verdict
  changing.

We call a verifier defect a *finding*. A mismatch that G4 attributes to
the verifier is a confirmed finding, because it comes from an executed
candidate. Some gates fail because of our environment rather than the
verifier, for example when the environment does not build or the
reference solution does not reach full marks in it. We call this a
*staging failure* and exclude the task instead of counting a defect.
Where the verifier is a pure function of the candidate, as the
deterministic components of $`\tau^{2}`$-bench are, G5 holds by
construction. All five gates were run on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench and
SWE-bench Verified. On Terminal-Bench and TB-Science only G1, G2 and G4
were run.

#### Certified tasks and candidates.

A task is *certified* when its suite passes the gates run on its
benchmark. A candidate is certified when its official verdict is not a
verifier defect under G4. Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
scores generated verifiers only on certified candidates of certified
tasks, and it takes the official verdict there as the *official label*
(Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "Labels. ‣ 4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")).
Certification is a necessary condition for a trustworthy label, not a
sufficient one. It shows that the verifier separates the candidates we
built, not every candidate an agent could produce.

### B.2 Benchmarks of Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")

For each benchmark of Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
this subsection gives how the candidates are built, what the official
verifier does with them, and what is certified.

#### $`\tau^{2}`$-bench.

The official verifier can compare the final database state with the
reference’s, check for expected calls, and check the agent’s messages
for required information by substring match. Each task declares which of
these count toward its reward. A further component, natural-language
assertions, needs a model judge, and no task counts it toward its
reward. For each of the 146 airline and banking tasks, we derived the
candidate suite mechanically from the task’s own golden actions and
executed every candidate in a fresh environment. On 89 tasks the
verifier has *full power*: the reference passes, the no-op fails, both
equivalents pass, and every near-miss is caught. On 33 other tasks the
verifier rejects the no-op but accepts at least one near-miss. On these
tasks it catches, on average, 53% of a task’s near-misses. So an agent
that skips one required step or gets one argument off by one is accepted
about half the time. On 24 tasks, all in the airline domain, the
reference solution makes no call that changes the database. A no-op
changes nothing either, so it passes the database comparison. These
tasks do not score expected calls. The only check left is for required
information in the agent’s messages, and on 23 of the tasks there is
none, so the no-op receives full marks. On these tasks the verifier
cannot tell a correct run from doing nothing. No task rejected an
equivalent. The 89 full-power tasks are the only $`\tau^{2}`$ tasks used
in Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
The candidates scored there are different: an agent’s run, the same run
without its last database-changing action, and the empty run, each
labeled by the official verifier.

#### SWE-bench Verified.

Correctness is defined by the tests attached to the pull request
\[[26](#bib.bib26), [42](#bib.bib42)\]. For Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
we gated 140 tasks from nine repositories. Each task has three
candidates: the gold patch, the no-op (empty) patch, and a corrupted
gold patch that drops one added line. The corrupted patch could be built
on 131 of the tasks. On every task the gold patch passes on all three
repeats, and when one of its tests is deleted, the suite exposes the
deletion. On 138 tasks the no-op and corrupted patches also fail on
every repeat. The two sympy tasks whose verdicts change between repeats
fail G5 and are excluded, leaving 138 certified tasks.

#### Terminal-Bench 4.0 and TB-Science 0.1.

Both benchmarks verify a task by running its own tests on the container
the agent leaves behind \[[36](#bib.bib36)\]. Both entered this paper
after the mechanisms of Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Core mechanisms ‣ 3 Veritas ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
were frozen. A candidate is the final state left by an episode run in
the task’s environment. The oracle runs the task’s reference script, and
the no-op runs nothing. Two further episodes run a cut version of the
reference script: *trunc* keeps its first three quarters, and *linedrop*
removes its last effectual line. Up to three corrupted candidates are
derived from the oracle’s final state. Each applies one of the following
operators to one output file, chosen by file type.

- C1
  multiplies the first numeric value by 1.1.
- C2
  removes a field or record.
- C3
  truncates the file to 90% of its size.
- C4
  changes the first match of \>=, \<=, == or True in a source file to
  \>, \<, != or False (on TB-Science also + to -).
- C5
  empties the file.
- C6
  multiplies a numeric value (for an array file, its first array) by 10,
  on TB-Science only.

The strength of each operator is fixed. These operators are generic.
They are not read from the verifier’s checks, so they test it less
sharply than candidates built from its source.

On Terminal-Bench the oracle fails its own tests in our environment on
22 of 66 tasks and yields no verdict on 10 more, and one environment
does not build. These 33 tasks are staging failures and are excluded. Of
the 70 TB-Science tasks \[[60](#bib.bib60)\], the oracle reaches full
marks in our environment on 40, and one of these fails to build for the
gate, leaving 39. On all 72 remaining tasks the no-op fails. Table
[7](#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Terminal-Bench 4.0 and TB-Science 0.1. ‣ B.2 Benchmarks of Section ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
gives, for each kind of candidate, the share that the official tests
accept. Of the 133 candidates derived from the oracle on Terminal-Bench,
the official tests reject 89 and accept 44. On TB-Science they reject
100 of 146 and accept 46. Of the accepted candidates, 15 on
Terminal-Bench and 18 on TB-Science are identical to the oracle in
effect. In these the cut removed only output, a check (such as echo or
test -f), a heredoc terminator, or nothing at all. The other 29 and 28,
which include 6 of the 7 Terminal-Bench candidates with a flipped
comparison, were adjudicated by hand under G4. In all, 34 of the 44
accepted candidates on Terminal-Bench and 41 of the 46 on TB-Science
meet every requirement of the task and keep their label. The other 10
and 5 violate a requirement the tests do not check. They are findings on
6 Terminal-Bench and 3 TB-Science tasks and are not certified, which
leaves 189 and 219 certified candidates.

|                | oracle | no-op | trunc | linedrop | C1   | C2   | C3  | C4  | C5   | C6   | all derived |
|----------------|--------|-------|-------|----------|------|------|-----|-----|------|------|-------------|
| Terminal-Bench | 33/33  | 0/33  | 9/33  | 15/32    | 4/12 | 4/13 | 3/7 | 6/7 | 3/29 | —    | 44/133      |
| TB-Science     | 39/39  | 0/39  | 20/39 | 13/28    | 5/19 | 0/20 | 0/2 | 5/8 | 0/11 | 3/19 | 46/146      |

Table 7: Candidates the official tests accept, by kind, on the 33
Terminal-Bench and 39 TB-Science tasks. C1–C6 are the corruption
operators listed above. Many accepted trunc and linedrop candidates are
identical to the oracle in effect. Seven TB-Science tasks have no
corrupted candidates: in five the corruption stage crashed, in one the
corrupted candidate’s image was missing when the verifiers ran, and one
produced none.

### B.3 Audit of official verifiers

Table
[8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ B.3 Audit of official verifiers ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
summarizes the defects that executed candidates confirm in the official
verifiers of six benchmarks. The rows for three of the four benchmarks
of Section
[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks")
come from Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Benchmarks of Section ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks").
This subsection describes the audit of the other three: Agents’ Last
Exam, DeepSWE and MCP-Atlas. Part of the audit is done by an LLM agent
that we call the *auditor*: it reads the source of a verifier that is a
program, writes candidates against it, and reports suspected defects as
findings. The defects run in both directions, too lenient and too
strict, but leniency dominates.

|  Benchmark |  Official verifier | Tasks |  Confirmed by execution |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Agents’ Last Exam \[[56](#bib.bib56)\] |  deterministic evaluator per task | 82 |  27 tasks accept a wrong candidate or reject a correct one |
|  $`\tau^{2}`$-bench \[[7](#bib.bib7), [55](#bib.bib55)\] |  state comparison + expected actions | 146 |  57 tasks lack full power: 33 reject the no-op but accept a near-miss; 24 more pass the no-op on the database comparison |
|  DeepSWE \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] |  hand-written checks per task | 106 |  36 tasks give full marks to the gold patch minus one hunk |
|  MCP-Atlas \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] |  one shared model judge | 500 |  72 tasks change verdict on identical input; 47 reject a correct paraphrase |
|  Terminal-Bench 4.0 \[[36](#bib.bib36)\] |  the task’s tests, run on the final state | 66 |  6 tasks accept a corrupted output that adjudication found defective |
|  TB-Science 0.1 \[[60](#bib.bib60)\] |  the task’s tests, run on the final state | 70 |  3 tasks accept a corrupted output that adjudication found defective |

Table 8: Confirmed defects in official verifiers. Every count is backed
by a candidate executed against the real verifier. Findings that
survived review but were not executed are counted separately in the
text. Task counts are the tasks audited (DeepSWE: after G5), not the
benchmark size.

#### Candidates from the verifier’s source.

Where the verifier is a program, the auditor reads its source and lists
the decision boundaries it implements. For each boundary it writes a
near-miss that crosses the boundary and an equivalent that stays inside
it. Both are written against the files the verifier actually reads.

#### Verification of findings.

The auditor also writes findings from the source, and these pass four
checks before they are counted. (i) The cited file and line must exist
and contain the code the finding describes. (ii) A second LLM agent, the
refuter, sees only the finding and the source and tries to refute it. It
may do so on six grounds: misread code, an unreachable entry point,
another check that would intervene first, behavior that is the intended
design, invented numbers, or overstated severity. Any doubt counts as
refutation. (iii) Surviving findings that can be expressed as a concrete
solution are executed against the real verifier and the real reference
solution. Before that, we check that the reference itself scores full
marks in our environment. A finding is confirmed only if its
counterexample scores as predicted. (iv) As a control on the auditor
itself, we ran it on a verifier written to be correct and on one with a
planted defect. It reported nothing on the first and found the plant in
the second.

#### Two tiers of findings.

A finding is *confirmed* only when a counterexample was executed against
the real verifier. It is *static* when it survived refutation but was
not executed. This typically happens because the reference solution did
not reach full marks in our environment, which makes the comparison
uninformative. Only confirmed findings appear in Table
[8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ B.3 Audit of official verifiers ‣ Appendix B Label Certification and Verifier Audit ‣ Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks"),
and static findings are counted in the paragraphs below.

#### Agents’ Last Exam.

ALE ships one deterministic evaluator per task and scores frontier
agents below one percent on its hardest tier \[[56](#bib.bib56)\]. We
audited the evaluators of the 82 public tasks that can be run
headlessly, about 43,000 lines of code. The auditor produced 723
findings. Of these, 715 cited code that exists and 158 survived
independent refutation. Of the 565 findings the refuter rejected, 83%
were rejected as intended design or overstated severity and 4% as
invented numbers or misread code. So the auditor errs toward severity,
not fabrication. Counterexamples for 70 findings were executed on the
real reference data. Of these, 36 were confirmed, 2 were refuted, 1
failed to run, and 31 were inconclusive because the reference solution
did not score full marks in our environment. Counting a task as
defective when at least one finding was confirmed by execution gives 27
of 82 tasks. Counting static findings as well gives 62. Among the 158
surviving findings, 91 make the evaluator too lenient and 29 too strict.
Another 19 omit a check the task requires, 14 crash or behave
undefinedly, and 5 are inconsistent or nondeterministic. The lenient
cases are the ones that matter for a reward signal. An ETL evaluator
compares five aggregate counts and never checks which customer a
transaction was assigned to, so it gives full marks when every
transaction is routed to “unknown customer”. A survival-analysis
evaluator checks the analysis script with five regular expressions over
its source, which a single dead-code line satisfies. It passes a
solution whose survival times are replaced by random numbers, and its R
script is never executed. A differential-expression evaluator computes
precision over true genes only, so false positives cost nothing. Other
evaluators omit a check the task requires: an option-pricing evaluator
never compares the exercise boundary, and an Ising evaluator checks no
physical invariant. In the other direction, one evaluator scores
standard SLURM syntax 0.

#### DeepSWE.

DeepSWE’s verifiers are hand-written to accept any implementation that
provides the requested functionality \[[24](#bib.bib24)\], which makes
them the strongest official verifiers we examined. Of the 113 tasks, 7
are excluded as staging failures. In 4 the reference solution does not
reach full marks in our environment, and in 3 its verdict is not stable
over three runs. For each remaining task we removed one hunk of the gold
patch at a time and scored the result. A hunk-removed patch is
incomplete by construction. On 36 of the 106 tasks at least one such
patch still receives full marks. Removing a single line instead of a
hunk gives a patch with full marks on 50 tasks. But on at least 18 of
them the removed line is a comment or documentation, so we report only
the hunk figure.

#### MCP-Atlas.

All 500 tasks share one model judge that scores an answer against atomic
factual claims \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], so its defects are shared too. The
candidates are the reference claims verbatim, the same input scored
twice at temperature zero, a correct paraphrase of the reference, and
numeric values four and six percent off. The last two lie on either side
of the five percent tolerance that the judge’s prompt states. Given the
reference claims verbatim, the judge marks all of them fulfilled on 475
tasks. Scored twice on identical input at temperature zero, it changes
its verdict on 72 tasks. Given a correct paraphrase of the reference, it
rejects 47. Values four percent off should pass, yet the judge fails
them on 100 tasks. Values six percent off should fail, yet it passes
them on 40.

$`\kappa^{*}`$ pools all candidates. Splitting them by kind shows which

Every plain harness and Veritas reject more than half of the reference
````
